tts: Your fridge doesn't actually make cold. It just pulls the heat out of your food and dumps it right into your kitchen.
That's why the back of it is warm. Touch it: that's the heat from your groceries.
The trick is the refrigerant. These days it's usually isobutane, which boils at just eleven degrees Fahrenheit.
In the freezer's tubes, it evaporates and soaks up heat from your food, the same way sweat cools your skin.
Then the compressor squeezes that vapor. It gets hot, and the coils on the back dump that heat into the room as it turns back into a liquid.
Next comes a tiny tube. The pressure drops, the liquid gets ice cold, and the loop starts all over again.
The first fridges ran on ammonia and sulfur dioxide, and the leaks were toxic. Then came freon, but it destroyed the ozone layer, so in nineteen eighty-seven the world started banning it.
So leaving the door open won't cool your kitchen. It'll actually heat it up. A fridge is really a heat pump.
